title: Reproduce it reliably before touching anything
story:
A failure is reported and the pressure is immediate, so somebody starts editing. Three speculative commits later the symptom has moved, the history is noise, and nobody can say whether anything was fixed — because there was never a way to make the failure happen on demand, so there is no way to tell a fix from a coincidence.

A failure you cannot reproduce is not yet a bug. It is a report of a bug. Until you have inputs, an environment and a state that trigger it whenever you ask, you do not have the thing you are trying to change, and any edit you make is being judged against a memory.

The clearest case of what reproduction is worth is the Ariane 5 maiden flight. On 4 June 1996, about forty seconds after the flight sequence began and at an altitude of around three thousand seven hundred metres, the launcher veered off its flight path, broke up and exploded. The Inquiry Board chaired by Jacques-Louis Lions reported that July.

The chain is worth following because every link is ordinary. The primary technical causes were an Operand Error converting the horizontal bias variable, and the lack of protection on that conversion, which stopped the computer of the inertial reference system. The alignment function producing that value was a legacy of Ariane 4 — meaningful only before liftoff, serving no purpose afterwards, and left running for fifty seconds after flight mode began. The value was much higher than expected because the early trajectory of Ariane 5 differs from that of Ariane 4 and produces considerably higher horizontal velocity. The analysis showing the conversion could not overflow was correct for the Ariane 4 trajectory. It simply did not hold for the new one, and it was jointly agreed not to include Ariane 5 trajectory data in the requirements at all.

Two further decisions made it fatal rather than merely wrong. Not all conversions were protected, because a maximum workload target of 80% had been set for the computer: seven variables were at risk, four were protected, and three including the horizontal bias were left alone on the judgement that they were physically limited or had a large safety margin. And the exception handling specified that on any exception the failure be flagged, the context stored, and the processor shut down — a decision the Board records as proving fatal, since restart is infeasible. Both modules failed, so the redundancy did not help.

Now the part this lesson is about. It would have been technically feasible to include almost the entire inertial reference system in the overall system simulations, and the simulated output was used instead of the system itself; had the system been included, the failure could have been detected. Afterwards the internal events were reproduced by simulation and the recovered memory pinned the context precisely. The failure was reproducible. Nobody had reproduced it.

problem.name: Deterministic reproduction
problem.shape: A failure has been reported and the only evidence of it is that it happened once, somewhere else.
tell: a fix has been attempted before the failure was made to happen on demand
the symptom moves rather than resolving
nobody can say what would count as evidence the bug is gone
the report is a screenshot or a recollection
problem.move: Establish inputs, environment and state that trigger the failure whenever you ask, and write it down as something runnable. Only then change code, because the reproduction is what any later change will be judged against — and if it resists reproduction, spend the effort on observability rather than on edits.
problem.invariant: Without a reproduction there is no way to distinguish a fix from a coincidence, because the only evidence that the failure stopped is that it has not happened again yet.
problem.breaks: Reproducibility in principle is not reproduction in practice, which is the whole content of the Ariane case: the failure was entirely deterministic and was reproduced afterwards by simulation, and none of that helped, because the reproduction was never run before the flight. A failure being reproducible is a property of the system; reproducing it is an act somebody has to perform.

cost.time: the slowest part of the work, performed before anything visibly improves, which is why it is the step under pressure to skip
cost.space: the fixtures, recorded inputs and environment definition needed to make the failure repeatable
cost.beats: speculative editing, which cannot be evaluated, and waiting for recurrence, which tells you the bug is still there without telling you anything else

worked.problem: The Ariane 5 failure was completely reproducible. Why did that not help?
worked.reasoning:
Because reproducible and reproduced are different things, and only the second requires somebody to do something.

The failure was deterministic. Given that trajectory, that alignment function and that unprotected conversion, the Operand Error happens every time. Afterwards it was reproduced by simulation, and the recovered memory allowed the failure context to be determined precisely. There was no randomness, no race, no timing dependence — nothing that would make it hard to trigger on demand.

What was missing was that nobody triggered it. The Board's finding is the one to carry: it would have been technically feasible to include almost the entire inertial reference system in the overall system simulations, but the simulated output of the system was used rather than the system itself, and had the system been included the failure could have been detected. The reproduction existed as a possibility the whole time and was never performed.

So the lesson generalises past rockets. A failure being reproducible is a property of the system. Reproducing it is an act. Teams routinely have the first and assume it substitutes for the second — the test exists but runs against a stub, the staging environment exists but differs in the one dimension that matters, the trajectory data exists but was jointly agreed not to be included in the specification.

That last one is worth dwelling on, because it is the most transferable part. The conversion had been analysed, and the analysis was correct — for the old trajectory. The new trajectory produced considerably higher horizontal velocity, and the analysis was never redone against it. The failure was not an unknown; it was a known thing checked against the wrong inputs.

Two things I would take into practice. First, when a component is expensive or awkward to include in a test, that is precisely the component whose exclusion will be load-bearing — the simulated output was used because using the real system was inconvenient, and the inconvenience is what hid the fault. Second, reproduction is what gives a later change something to be judged against; without it, the evidence that a fix worked is that the failure has not happened again yet, which is also the evidence that it was never fixed.

problem.practice: Take a bug you are currently working on and try to make it happen on demand, writing down the exact inputs, environment and state. If you cannot, stop and note what is missing — that gap is the work. Then look at your test suite for a component replaced by a stub because including it was awkward.

beats.broke: A failure is reported and the pressure is to act, so code gets edited before anyone can make the failure happen on demand — after which nothing distinguishes a fix from a coincidence.
beats.fix: Establish a reproduction first: the exact inputs, environment and state that trigger the failure whenever you ask, so any later change has something to be judged against.
beats.cost: Reproduction is the slowest part and feels like not fixing, and the failures that most need it — the intermittent ones — are exactly the ones that resist it.

interview.q: The Ariane 5 failure was completely reproducible. Why did that not help?
interview.trap: Treating it as a coding error that better review would have caught. The conversion had been analysed and the analysis was correct — for the previous trajectory. It was a known thing checked against the wrong inputs, and the system that would have exposed it was left out of the simulation because including it was inconvenient.
interview.answer:
Because reproducible and reproduced are different things, and only the second requires somebody to do something.

The failure was deterministic: given that trajectory, that alignment function and that unprotected conversion, the Operand Error happens every time. It was reproduced afterwards by simulation, and recovered memory allowed the failure context to be determined precisely. No randomness, no race, nothing that would make it hard to trigger.

The Board's finding is the one to carry: it would have been technically feasible to include almost the entire inertial reference system in the overall system simulations, but the simulated output was used rather than the system itself — and had the system been included, the failure could have been detected. The reproduction was available the whole time and was never performed.

So it generalises past rockets. Reproducible is a property of the system; reproducing is an act. Teams routinely have the first and assume it substitutes for the second — the test exists but runs against a stub, staging exists but differs in the one dimension that matters, the trajectory data exists but was jointly agreed not to be included in the specification.

That last point is the most transferable. The conversion had been analysed and the analysis was correct — for the Ariane 4 trajectory. Ariane 5 produced considerably higher horizontal velocity and the analysis was never redone. It was not an unknown; it was a known thing checked against the wrong inputs.

Two things I would take into practice. When a component is expensive or awkward to include in a test, that is precisely the component whose exclusion will be load-bearing — the simulated output was used because using the real system was inconvenient, and the inconvenience is what hid the fault. And reproduction is what gives a later change something to be judged against: without it, the evidence a fix worked is that the failure has not recurred yet, which is also the evidence it was never fixed.
